title: why people stand up when the book comes in
hookLine: why people stand up when the book comes in

cards: A guest at a Catholic Mass spends a lot of it half a second behind. Everyone else seems to know when to sit, when to stand, when to kneel, and the guest is watching the person in front.
One moment in particular catches visitors off guard. People have been sitting quietly, listening to readings. Then music starts, often the word alleluia, and the whole room stands up at once.
Someone at the front lifts a book up high. Why stand for a book? Day two was the table at the center of the Mass.
Today, the first half: the story.

teach.b: First, the name. The word Mass is usually traced to the old Latin words at the end of the service, ite, missa est, roughly: go, you are sent. So the whole thing may be named for the moment people walk back out the door.
Now, the first half. Catholics call it the Liturgy of the Word, and it's mostly listening.

teach.h: READINGS, A PSALM, THEN THE GOSPEL.
teach.b: On a Sunday there's usually a reading from the Old Testament, then a psalm, often sung back and forth, then a reading from one of the letters of the apostles. People sit for those.

Then comes the Gospel, a reading from one of the four books about the life of Jesus, and everyone stands. The English word Gospel goes back to an Old English phrase for good news, and it translates the Greek euangelion.
Catholics say that when the Gospel is read, Christ himself is speaking to the people gathered there. So you stand the way you'd stand when someone important walks into the room.
Right before it, people trace three little crosses with a thumb: on the forehead, on the lips, on the heart. It's day one's sign, shrunk down.
One common way to explain it: may these words be in my mind, on my lips, in my heart. Standing for the reading isn't new, either.

teach.h: EZRA OPENS THE BOOK. THEY STAND.
teach.b: In the Bible itself, after the exile, the scribe Ezra opens the book of the law in front of the whole people, and when he opens it, they all stand up. Then everyone sits again, and a priest or deacon preaches: the homily.
The story has entered the room.

how: At Mass, Catholics sit for the first readings and the psalm, then stand for the Gospel, often tracing small crosses on the forehead, lips and heart as it is announced.

games.q: what happens in the first half — tap the pairs.
p: opened the book; the people stood

s: the name Mass is usually traced to a Latin phrase about being sent
from the old ending, ite, missa est: go, you are sent.
people stand for every reading at Mass
they sit for the first readings and stand for the Gospel.
standing for the reading is described in the Bible itself
in Nehemiah, the people stand when Ezra opens the book.

games.q: you're in the crowd when the scribe Ezra lifts the book of the law and opens it in front of everyone. what do the people do?
o: they cover their faces and sit.
games.why: when he opened the book, all the people stood. Catholics still stand when the Gospel is read.

practice: Here's the practice. If you're sitting, stand up, just for this, the way the room stands for the Gospel. Touch your forehead, your lips, your heart.
Then sit back down, breathe slowly, and let each of those three places get ready to listen. You don't have to say anything.

wordCard.voice: The Gospel. The good news: the reading about the life of Jesus that everyone stands to hear, the high point of the Mass's first half. Twelfth word.

orig.note: Latin: go, you are sent (literally, it is the sending). the dismissal that gave the Mass its name.

carryVoice: Your line: the story enters the room. That's why everyone gets to their feet. Day twelve.

sources.ref: General Instruction of the Roman Missal, on the Liturgy of the Word
